newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav army chief hints at support for protests.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav army chief hints at support for protests.

text.p: The Yugoslav army commander met students in the Serbian opposition movement on Monday and indirectly backed their campaign to restore opposition election victories annulled by President Slobodan Milosevic.

Seven consecutive weeks of pro-democracy street protests have shaken his authoritarian Socialist government, and the West has warned him that Yugoslavia faces indefinite international isolation unless he moves towards democracy.

Sympathy for the opposition's cause from General Momcilo Perisic, chief of the Yugoslav army general staff, was the latest crack in the 50-year-old monolith of leftist rule in rump Yugoslavia, made up of only Serbia and tiny Montenegro.
Perisic told the student delegation that under the constitution the army stayed out of politics. But he said he favoured a democratic solution to the crisis that would help Yugoslavia rejoin Europe.

"General Perisic underlined the Yugoslav Army's... special interest in seeing that all current problems are overcome within the legal institutions of the system in a manner deployed in democratic countries," an army statement released by the official news agency Tanjug said.
Such an approach was necessary to secure Yugoslavia's re-entry to the international community, it said.
Last October the United Nations repealed sanctions imposed on Yugoslavia in 1992 for its fomenting of war in Bosnia.

But the West wants to see democratic and free-market reforms in Yugoslavia before it funnels in money sought by Milosevic to reconstruct its wrecked economy and readmits Belgrade to key international institutions.

The army's message was couched in terms that avoided open endorsement of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition. But it effectively criticised Milosevic's annulment of the elections by demanding respect for international democratic norms.
An inquiry by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) verified opposition claims to have won voting in 15 of Serbia's 18 largest cities including Belgrade.

Serbia's Socialist government grudgingly admitted last week that Zajedno had won in a few of the smaller cities but insisted that in other districts no party gained a majority or the results were inconclusive and needed further study.

Cedomir Jovanovic, spokesman for the five-member student delegation that met Perisic for 30 minutes, said the general bolstered the opposition's campaign by calling for the rule of law to be observed in Serbia.
"We have found ourselves on the same side since both they and we demand that the constitution be observed," Jovanovic told independent Belgrade radio B-92.
Dusan Vasiljevic, another student leader, said Perisic promised "no repeat of 1991" when Milosevic ordered tanks into Belgrade to crush demonstrations for democratic change.
Milosevic alienated the army by summarily purging scores of generals and running down the ranks after the forces failed to prevent Croatia's secession from federal Yugoslavia in 1991.
Last week, unidentified army officers warned Milosevic after he unleashed riot police to beat demonstrators that army troops would not fire on protesters again.
The opposition movement has also garnered sympathy from the Serbian Orthodox Church and disgruntled elements of the police, whose standard of living has plunged like most Yugoslavs.
After seeing Perisic, the five student leaders were received by Serbian Interior Minister Zoran Sokolovic but said the meeting proved "completely unproductive".

They said Sokolovic refused to lift a ban on street marches imposed after a December 24 riot between Zajedno supporters and SPS loyalists. Police have since confined protesters to squares and pedestrian malls, ostensibly to prevent traffic jams.

Zajedno circumvented the anti-march edict on Sunday by arriving for their daily rally in thousands of cars moving at snail's pace, causing a vast traffic jam and allowing more than 100,000 protesters to flood the streets.
Police did not intervene and there was no violence.

Demonstrators planned to gather on Monday evening in Republic Square and then march to St Sava's cathedral for midnight mass. The Serbian Orthodox Church celebrates Christmas on January 7 according to the old Julian calendar.
